newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain under pressure as BSE debate rages.
newsitem.headline: Britain under pressure as BSE debate rages.

text.p: Britain will come under renewed pressure from its European partners this week to start culling more cattle in the public health scare over mad cow disease.

Separately, EU farm ministers are expected at a two-day meeting starting on Monday to reject a proposal to ban tissue from sheep, goats and cattle believed to be infected with either scrapie or mad cow disease, EU diplomats said.

Britain's partners are waiting for it to comply with an agreement at the EU summit in Florence in June to cull up to 147,000 cattle most at risk to the disease as part of a deal for a gradual lifting of a global ban on British beef exports.
The EU imposed the ban in March after London disclosed that the disease, which has killed around 165,000 British cattle over the past 10 years, could spread to people who ate infected beef.
"It (the cull) would be long overdue," European Commission farm spokesman Gerard Kiely said. "The ball is in their court."

EU farm ministers will be looking for a signal when British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg on Tuesday issues a progress report on the fight against the disease, known medically as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
Kiely said it was up to Britain to come forward with a proposal which would be examined by EU scientific committees before any decision could be taken on easing the ban.
"It's impossible to say how long it would take," he added.

Recent British and French research has shown that people could catch the human variant of BSE, known as Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), from eating meat infected with scrapie -- a similar brain-wasting disease widespread in sheep.

Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, who has been criticised for listening too much to farmers, says that protection of human health and the restoration of consumer confidence must be given priority. He insists member states should act likewise.

But by using a special voting procedure, ministers look set to endorse, probably on Tuesday, the view of senior national veterinary officials and throw out the European Commission's proposal by a simple majority of eight member states.
"That looks very likely," a diplomat said.

Earlier this month, 12 members of the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee voted against the proposal, saying the measures were economically unjustified as their countries were virtually free of scrapie and mad cow disease.
Britain and France voted in favour. Ireland abstained.
Since then only Portugal has shifted its stance, saying it will now abstain, diplomats said.
The EU Commission has proposed that the brains, eyes, spinal cord and spleen should be removed from sheep, goats and cattle over 12 months old and kept out of human and animal food.
Other animal parts, such as the liver, are deemed safe.

The EU's executive, worried that it will be savaged by a European Parliament committee of inquiry for mishandling the mad cow, or Bovine Spongioform Encephalopathy (BSE) crisis, wants to take the initiative and shift the blame onto member states.
Ironicaly, Germany, which has been the most insistent on tough public health measures, is now holding back.
Backed by a majority, it argues that the measures are excessive in countries that are virtually free of the disease and where stringent national controls exist.
"Fischler has gone overboard," another diplomat said.
